newsitem.title: USA: GRAIN SORGHUM--Earworms could reduce U.S. yields.
newsitem.headline: GRAIN SORGHUM--Earworms could reduce U.S. yields.

text.p: An unusually heavy infestation of earworms could reduce sorghum yields in Texas, Oklahoma and southern Kansas unless producers remain vigilant about spraying for the insects, crop experts said Tuesday.

Tim Lust, director of marketing for National Grain Sorghum Producers, said the earworm problem was particularly heavy in the Texas and Oklahoma panhandles and in southern Kansas. Lust estimated that earworms had infested between 20 and 30 percent of all U.S. sorghum acreage.
"It is a problem that this area normally does not see...but a little bit of late crop, a lot of moisture and a lot of grain means we are seeing some of it this year," Lust said.
"So far it's been very easily controlled," he said. "I don't see it having any impact at all on total sorghum production, except that it's costing farmers several dollars an acre to go in and spray."
Gary Strickland, Oklahoma State University area research and extension specialist for the Oklahoma Panhandle, warned that this year's problem was serious because of the high number of worms per head.

"We've seen as many as two to four per head in the heavy spots and we've seen fields that do not have quite one per head," Strickland said. "That's notable. Corn earworms are cannibalistic and to find more than one per head indicates that you do have high pressure."
Strickland said the first generation of worms consume the florets of the plant as it emerges from the boot stage, and successive generations feed on kernels.
"If producers do not check (and spray) their fields... they can lose as much as 10 percent of the potential yield," Strickland said.

Kansas is typically the leading U.S. sorghum producer, followed by Nebraska and Texas. But acreage in Oklahoma was running ahead of normal this year because many producers switched to sorghum when their winter wheat acres failed.

During the week ended Sunday, the Kansas sorghum crop was rated 87 percent good to excellent, 12 percent fair and one percent poor, according to the weekly crop report released Monday by the Kansas Agricultural Statistics Service.
That marked an increase over the previous week's rating of 85 percent good to excellent, 12 percent fair and three percent poor to very poor.
